speechtext:
All of us can take pride in the fact that for the first time in Canada's immigration legislation we have a clear-cut definition of refugees and also a claim for refugee status. All members of the committee wanted to see this incorporated into the act. It is pleasing to see, after many representations from various interest groups across the country, that a refugee policy has been incorporated into the bill. Members of the United Nations Commission on refugees feel that it is a forerunner of refugee legislation.
From time to time too much stress has been placed on the so-called civil liberties of persons who have been on the fringes of a criminal element. It has concerned me that these people should be afforded every civil liberty. On the other hand there were members of the committee who seemed to stress the civil liberties of these persons over the protection of Canadians. This government has lost the handle on immigration. Canada's immigration laws have not been administered strongly enough. People have come into Canada and used Canada as a base to continue their criminal activities. I am referring to a very small number of people. That is not part of immigration and it should not be accepted by Canadians.
The minister's powers in this new legislation should prevent the criminal element from coming into Canada. He has the power to deport, and that is what is expected of him. It has nothing to do with the landing of bona fide immigrants who want to come to this country and start a new life, thus giving us the benefit of their experience and their ability. It has nothing to do with persons who try to exploit this country and beat the law. That is not what we want to see in the act. Criticism has been strongly levelled at the minister. He should use the act in such a manner that criminals will not use Canada as a base for their activities. It is for this reason we have endorsed clauses which may be wide-reaching and discretionary, new clauses regarding organized crime, terrorists and hijacking. This is an ongoing phenomenon in our modern world, and we need a law whereby the minister and his officials can act quickly and forcibly to protect Canadian society.
There is one other matter that I want to bring to the attention of the House tonight, and that is the matter of immigrant selection. Hon. members opposite know that I have favoured an immigration selection system based on the point system whereby we would have a sponsored class, a refugee class, and an independent class. The minister and his officials also know that we have recommended the expansion of the sponsored class and the removal of the nominated class. One might say that that means that one is opposed to such objectives as timely reunification. That is not the case. I believe that the reunification of next of kin, of those within the nuclear

family, is well taken care of in the sponsored class, especially if we expand it to the sponsorship of parents of any age.
I am concerned that with the point system as it is now retained what will happen is that the percentage of the total flow of the so-called nominated class will increase to the point where independent immigrants will have a very difficult time in coming into Canada. There is a distinct advantage for a person getting points to have some family relationship. What I would have preferred is that all those apply as independent immigrants. They would then come into the country, it is true, and adjust to Canadian society with the assistance of their families. I feel very strongly that we will see the day when the sponsor of the refugee class will take such a high proportion of our annual flow that the independent immigrant who is willing to go to areas outside our cities-and studies show this is the group that has frequently gone to the outlying areas-will have much greater difficulty coming to this country, and I do not believe our immigration policy should be structured in that way.
In conclusion I would like to say that we have a better bill than before, a better immigration policy, and members of this House are pleased to see the end of the exercise. It is for that reason we will be supporting it on final reading.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I tried to make clear in the debate on second reading, and indeed in discussions in the committee, that I am quite prepared to admit that there are some features of the present legislation which are satisfactory, and improvements on what we had before, and I am also prepared to admit that the committee produced some useful amendments. Nevertheless, we think we have a bad bill and we should vote against it.
There are three areas in which the bill is unsatisfactory. First, the bill contains provisions which seriously jeopardize the right to proper hearings and fundamental freedoms. The main sections which are unsatisfactory are found in Clauses 19 and 27 dealing with reports against persons in Canada providing for their removal or deportation. I will not go over the whole argument in respect of Clause 19-members of the committee have heard me speak on it more than once and they must probably be getting a little tired of it-but the difficulty is that Clause 19 gives the right to refuse admission on the basis of speculative opinions and suspicions of immigration officers. This is in direct contradiction of what was previously in the Immigration Act. It was only when a person was convicted of certain kinds of criminal acts, or admitted to the commission of such acts, that he or she might be deported.
It has long been a basic principle of justice as it is known in Canada that a person should not be penalized for things he might do at some future time but has not done. What he is likely to do is purely a matter of speculation, and it is wrong that a person should be condemned, with the severe consequence of deportation, on the basis of committing one or more indictable offences, when some of these offences are relatively trivial. Nor should persons be liable to deportation because an immigration officer believes that there are reasonable grounds to assume that such a person will engage in subversion by force
July 25, 1977

of any government. Any democratic government would have some sympathy for them, but some Canadian immigrants come from countries in which brutal dictatorships deny fundamental human rights, deny any possibility of a peaceful change, and indeed engage in widespread torture. The previous act dealt with this matter by referring to democratic governments, and I am prepared to see our immigration law seeking to protect democratic governments, but I see no reason why we should seek to protect regimes such as the one in Uganda at present, or those in some parts of South America and other parts of the world.
Another subclause makes liable to deportation a person who is a member of or is likely to participate in local activities and organizations likely to engage in such acts of violence. In the world as we know it today there are many organizations in different parts of the world engaged in many different ways of doing things. In other parts of the world there are people who are held down by violence and terror, and if they desire to change these regimes in order to assist their country, that is no good reason for Canada to refuse them admission. But it is quite possible that members of these organizations in Canada know nothing about the so-called violent activities of other members of an organization in another section of the world- they are perfectly innocent of any offence, and to penalize a person who is not knowingly guilty of any offence is wrong. It is what people do in Canada that should be of importance.
Clause 27 provides that where a person other than a Canadian citizen or permanent resident obtains entry by reason of any fraud or improper means of representation or any material fact, he or she can be deported. The American clause that covers this refers to wilful misrepresentation of any material facts. Our courts have interpreted an act similar to Clause 27(h) as applying even where the misrepresentation of material facts is without any intent to deceive. It is indeed a harsh penalty to refuse admission in such a case.
Every police officer, every immigration officer, is given the power to arrest without a warrant. The need to secure a warrant is a reasonable protection. It can usually be obtained on an affidavit or other sworn document. The deputy minister or senior immigration officer may issue such a warrant on reasonable grounds. Therefore there should be no difficulty for an immigration officer seeking to make an arrest in securing a warrant, and this would give adequate protection by having two different people, a senior member of the department or an immigration officer, look into the question of whether there is a proper basis for detention. It is extremely dangerous to give this power allowing wide groups of people, some trained and some not trained, to arrest on their own initiative at any time of the day or night. It removes a most important bulwark to hasty and ill-considered arrests.
The act still contains some provisions to permit fingerprinting, although it does not apply them with uniformity. People who come from the United States or the United Kingdom do not require visas and therefore are not liable to be fingerprinted. I am not personally very violently against fingerprinting, but it has been associated with criminal activities, and it is
Immigration
wrong for it to be required for certain classes of immigrants and not required for other immigrants. One thing that adds to the vice of deporting people on the grounds of suspicion is that the right of appeal to the Immigration Appeal Board is severely limited. In order to be sure of proper hearings all cases of deportation should be subject to appeal.
The second major objection we have was mentioned at second reading. That is that some of the most important provisions with respect to immigrants are delegated to the governor in council, and any parliamentary control, even of some of the key factors, is done away with.
Clause 115 deals with the making of regulations. There are 18 different classes of matters. Some of these are matters of detail, and it is perfectly reasonable to make rules and regulations without reference to parliament, but there are three subclauses in Clause 115(a) which provide for the establishment and application of selection criteria based on such factors as family relationships, education, and skill.
I do not need to read the whole group of things which are to be taken into account. At the very core of the Immigration Act are the standards by which we admit people, yet that is not delegated to parliament, and parliament has no real input whatever into the process.
Clause 115(b) deals with sponsored applicants. We say very piously in Clause 3 that one of the main purposes of the bill is to aid in the reunion of families. Then, instead of insisting that the rules in this respect be set out by acts of parliament so that they can be seen by all, we say that the rules with respect to this shall be delegated to the governor in council. Of course we do not really mean the governor in council. We know that the governor in council does not have time to deal with all these immigration matters. We mean the people who advise the Minister of Manpower and Immigration.
By changing the regulations the government on a number of occasions has totally changed the law and caused the number of immigrants to vary very widely either up or down. Some of this may be necessary, but the important laws should be made by parliament. I tried in two amendments to introduce provisions which would enable parliament to intervene. The first was to define "family" for the purposes of sponsorship by setting out precise relationships.
The second amendment I proposed was that any regulations passed under Clause 115(a), (b) and (c) could be brought before parliament by a petition of 20 members, to be followed by debate and recorded vote within a certain limited time. This would make it necessary that all regulations under (a), (b) or (c) would be reviewed in parliament where 20 members are sufficiently concerned to take action by petition to secure parliamentary approval. The difference between the minister and my party on this lies in our evaluation of the role and supremacy of parliament. There are, of course, many other clauses of the bill which are to be dealt with by regulation.
As far as the principle of acceptance of refugees is concerned the minister said that we have a wonderful scheme for

July 25, 1977
Immigration
refugees, but no member of the committee knows what it is because it is in regulations which have not been published. We really do not know whether his words of praise for the regulations or proposals are justified or not justified. Terms and conditions which may be imposed on immigrants when they come to Canada are to be dealt with by regulation, and they are yet to be prescribed. I could go through the bill and find time and time again the reference in clauses "as prescribed by the regulations".
One of the difficulties of having everything done by regulations is the lack of public knowledge or, in fact, the secrecy with which some of these regulations are dealt. The minister did, as he has told us, indeed cause an amendment to Clause 115 to be proposed which provided that regulations passed under subclauses (a), (b) or (c) would not come into force unless published in the Canada Gazette. However, the Canada Gazette is packed with volumes of material, and it is almost impossible to find anything in it. I defy a layman or a new immigrant to be able to make head or tail of what is in the Canada Gazette. It would be extremely difficult to find the relevant provisions. The average immigrant would be completely at a loss, even if he did find the appropriate regulation. They are often highly complicated. The amendments I proposed were turned down, so we did not have and will not have a direct parliamentary say in these crucial matters.
There are one or two other matters I would like to call to the attention of the House. One has to do with security matters. These are very elaborate provisions allowing the minister or the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) to give certificates, and an advisory board to make recommendations, and then for the governor in council to order deportation after considering the reports of the special advisory board.
The weakness of all this is that what should be a matter of judicial power is given to political officers. I think that is quite wrong. It is wrong to say that procedures could not be devised which would enable a review of these cases by judicial officers. During the last war the defence of Canada regulations were passed giving to the then minister of justice, Mr. Louis St. Laurent, the power to detain and intern persons who, in his opinion, might be dangerous to the state. A fairly large number of persons was so detained. Eventually, however, parliament approved of a change whereby county and superior court judges could have hearings in such cases, and provision was made in cases where information was confidential not to publicize the sources of that information. This system worked perfectly well, and many persons were released. No difficulties seemed to result. I proposed such an amendment in straightforward terms to this section of the present act. This again was turned down.
The minister has developed a habit of saying that if a change is made, it would be a threat to the whole administration of the Immigration Act. What we have been primarily concerned about has been fairness and justice so that human beings facing the prospects of deportation can have fair hearings and an opportunity to meet the cases against them.
[Mr. Brewin.J
One other clause has been mentioned by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp). I find that clause very strange indeed. Clause 3 sets out the purposes of Canadian immigration policy and includes, as one of the main purposes, enriching and strengthening the cultural and social fabric of Canada, taking into account the federal and bilingual character of Canada. I proposed an amendment which would have added the multicultural nature of Canada. I was, of course, referring to the thousands of people-nay, perhaps millions-who come to Canada from countries other than Britain and France.
I am told that there are as many as perhaps three million from different ethnic backgrounds in Canada. They are particularly concerned about the management of immigration. Many of them have not been in this country very long, and they still have friends and relatives in the countries from which they came. There is a general statement of purpose in Clause 3, and I think it justifies consultation with these groups. As a matter of fact, some of the very best recommendations the committee received were from some of the so-called ethnic, multicultural groups. They have a right to be interested. They are not second class citizens. They are Canadians. We are all Canadians together, and no differences of culture should provide even a verbal exclusion of these people.
I am sure there are many other things that can be said about the bill. I am trying to bring out the salient features. I would like to finish by saying two things. First, we must always remember when discussing immigration that we are dealing with persons, human beings. It is all very well to be practical, to look into the economics and consider our own security. However, we must also in our own interests look at the human side of these problems.
These, therefore, are my three main objections. First is Clause 19 which condemns people on speculation and suspicion. Second is the refusal to recognize that the regulations are often not the right way to deal with key parts of the statute. The third is the recognition of the multicultural nature of Canada. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the motion be amended by striking out all the words after the word "That", and by substituting therefor the following words:
"Bill C-24, An Act respecting immigration to Canada, be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration for the purpose of reconsidering Clauses 3, 19 and 115 thereof.".

Mr. Speaker, 1 begin by saying it would be a great disservice to the country if the motion proposed by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) were passed. It is time that we passed this measure to give Canadians the immigration bill for which they have waited much too long.
On second reading debate I could not find it within my convictions to support this bill. I felt that the measures in it were far too open ended. They gave the minister too much power to change the immigration policy of the government simply by altering regulations with little reference to parliament, only by order in council.
That kind of power has distorted the demographics of Canada for the past 15 years. We do not need to extend that power now. For that reason, and for the reason of the loose definition of the family, I felt it was a very poor bill and could not vote in favour of it.
Having worked in committee and having seen some of the amendments that have been passed, I am pleased to see what has happened and the openness on the part of the minister to accept amendments. Therefore I am in favour of what is happening, even though the bill is still imperfect in many ways.
If we are going to talk about immigration, we need to concern ourselves with two very important principles. First, in looking at an immigration policy for Canada we must look to further the interests and welfare of Canada. That is our responsibility. I am very concerned about the humanitarian objectives that we as Canadians need to espouse and cultivate in our country.
It seems to me that those who are interested in coming to Canada are interested in Canada for one reason. Our country is different from theirs. They not only come here because Canada is attractive to them but because the place in which
Immigration
they are is unattractive to them. They want to leave the circumstances in which they find themselves.
If we are to preserve an attractive country we must preserve the characteristics which made it attractive and which we enjoy today. In order to do this we must maintain a sensitive control of immigration flow. For this reason I would be happier if the regulations were contained in the bill. Nevertheless, I am pleased to see that one of the amendments, an amendment to Clause 3, calls for the rules and regulations made by the immigration department to be in conformity with the objectives of the bill. have the right to the opinion of a competent health specialist in addition to that of the examining doctor. speechtext:
Yes, perhaps a ghost writer did that for him- and it will come back to haunt him. The minister of health was looking after his own welfare and that of his bureaucrats when he revised that policy. Representations were brought to us by the National Association of the Mentally Retarded. They said it was easy enough for an immigration officer to betray his bias when examining an immigrant, and that it was not fair that the fate of an application should rest upon the opinion of one medical officer; there should be the right of recourse to the opinion of a specialist. But the minister of health knows better than those who specialize in various areas. He has never dealt with these cases. He has never been in contact with a family whose child might be retarded, or considered as being retarded. Because he is a Rhodes scholar he has never entered into the world of such a family or felt for its needs.
I think it is a shame that the minister has seen fit to bring in an amendment which waters down the protection afforded to applicants in such cases. The principle is the right to know. Under present circumstances when a case rests upon the opinion of one medical officer there is no way in which an applicant can feel sure his application is being rejected fairly. Under the amendment which unfortunately the House has just passed, the application simply goes to a second medical officer, a process which does nothing for the applicant and gives him no extra protection. All it means is a shuffling of folders and application forms in some immigration office overseas.
If we are to be fair, we must eliminate bias and prejudice. It is all too easy in the world in which we live for an immigration officer in any country abroad to get tired of looking at applications, tired of making decisions. In this connection, I think of the line which reads: "And wretches hang that jurymen may dine". I can offer the House a perfect illustration.
Some time ago a constituent of mine came to see me, with his wife. They are from India. They wanted to enter Canada but they had a teen-aged son who suffered from a serious heart condition. The medical officer examining them said the rest of the family could enter as immigrants but the son could not pass the medical test because of his heart condition. In view of the exigencies of the family's situation in India, the family decided to come to Canada and leave the child in the care of

an uncle. The uncle formally adopted him so that the rest of the family could come here.
Once here, naturally they were lonesome for their son. They earned enough money to supply him with an air ticket so that he could visit them. While he was here they took him to a heart specialist. The heart specialist said he had a very severe problem but that the operation was not very severe and the boy could be taken care of very quickly. This they proceeded to do; the young boy underwent an operation and was cured 100 per cent. The family wants to bring him to Canada but he is now a member of a different family. If the minister had adopted the amendment we put forward in committee that would not have happened. The medical officer would have been required to pass the application on to the responsible medical specialist who would have said that he could take care of it. A general practitioner would not have looked at the matter.
The minister of health who is supposed to be looking after the welfare of people I say has done a disservice to some Canadians as well as discriminated against some who want to come to Canada to join their families. He has displayed his bias, and 1 say shame on him.
I do not want to prolong the debate. 1 just want to bring to the attention of hon. members what we have done to some families who want to come to Canada. They have been done harm. We have talked about prejudice. People come to my office every month who seem to think that prejudice exists in the immigration system. People from England say that it would be easier to reunite their families if they were from some country other than England. They believe there is prejudice. It is time that we made our immigration policy as open as possible in the sense of information, so that both by statute and by published regulations people know how their applications to come to Canada will be judged.
That is all I have to say, Mr. Speaker. I trust we will end this debate soon and give the Canadian people the Immigration Act that they deserve.

Mr. Speaker, 1 have no intention of keeping the House very long, although I think we could have done without the motion which was moved a few moments ago.
I have been surprised at some of the comments which the minister made. It is true that both at second reading stage and in committee there was a great deal of discussion and exchange of opinions among members. Representations were made by a very wide variety of organizations. However, I cannot agree with the minister when he suggests that the committee approached questions with an open mind. He inferred, if he did not actually say so, that the committee reached a consensus. Anyone who has read the minutes of the meetings will realize that there were many submissions made by organizations which were not accepted by the government. A similar fate befell many of the most important suggestions
July 25, 1977

and draft amendments made by members from all parties, including members on the government side.
We oppose this bill for the reason which some of us outlined at the report stage in some detail, as did my colleague the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) tonight. We believe that the bill gives much too much power and authority to the department and its officials. This does not mean that we think the policy in past years has been bad. It does not mean that we think we have permitted too many people to come to Canada or that we believe that the wrong kind of people have come to Canada. We just do not believe that any individuals or departments should be given the power virtually over life and death that is given in this bill to those who work for the government.
We do not believe, as we have made clear at all stages of debate that regulations drafted by public servants and adopted by cabinet, regulations which are not discussed or debated in parliament, are the way to formulate immigration policy.
I do not believe that this bill is as good as its proponents have suggested. Nor do I believe it is as bad as its opponents say. 1 have had representations made to me by constituents, as 1 am sure have many members from city constituencies, particularly constituencies in cities where there has been large scale immigration, to the effect that there has not been enough debate. I do not believe that is true, but they believe it is because there has been relatively little media reporting of the debates which have taken place in the House and in committee on this bill.
They believe that this bill will cut off immigration and that it will stop their friends and relatives from coming to Canada in the future. I do not believe that, but that is the way they feel. Nor do I believe, as 1 have said, that the bill is as good as the minister and members on the government side claim.
We are living in a changing world. Our open immigration policy is bound to change in the next few years. I doubt that there is a single member-certainly there is not a party in parliament-who does not believe that such a change is inevitable and who would not support such a change. After all, no other country in the world has taken in the number of immigrants Canada has, at least in percentage terms. This country has always been a country of immigrants.
Since the end of World War II more than three million people have come to Canada. Prior to World War II, and for four or five years after the war, almost all of the immigrants who came to Canada were either from Great Britain or countries in northern Europe. This began to change in the 1950's when we saw large scale immigration to Canada of people from countries such as Italy, and later Spain and Portugal. In more recent years we have seen a very large inflow of immigrants from countries which in earlier times never provided immigrants to this country, namely, countries in the West Indies, India, Pakistan, Hong Kong and Africa.
We Canadians have had to learn, and are still learning to live in close proximity with people whose language, colour and religion are different from those to which we have been accustomed. On the whole, that adjustment has been easy and
Immigration
smooth and Canadians have accepted the changes which have taken place. But there have been other changes. Immigrants who came to Canada before World War I to a large extent, at least in western Canada, became farmers. They came to open up land which had not been worked prior to their arrival. Their children and grandchildren can be found in almost every part of western Canada.
Today's immigrants will work in our cities, mostly Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver. Some people express surprise about that. There has been talk to devise policies encouraging people to come to Canada, provided they will not move to our large cities. That will not be possible because when they opt for large cities they are following the example of people resident in Canada. They want to go to the large cities because that is where the action is and that is where the jobs are.
The number of immigrants coming to Canada will decline. According to Statistics Canada, we have about 900,000 unemployed. In fact we are aware that there are substantially more than one million unemployed. Faced with that kind of situation and the pressure for housing and other facilities in the city, people living in Canada, including the children and granchil-dren of immigrants, are saying to members of parliament that Canada should slow down the number of immigrants it permits to come into this country. 1 do not believe anyone would disagree with that policy, but a reduction will not take place as a result of this bill.
Reduction can occur if the government changes regulations, as it has done in the past when it desired a reduction in the number of immigrants. A reduction can be achieved by changing the staffing of immigration officers in the countries from which people want to emigrate. If we want to reduce the number of immigrants, we have to cut the staff by 25 per cent or 50 per cent, thus enabling them to process a lesser number of immigrants wanting to come to Canada. We do not object to a reduction, but we object to the reduction which will take place under a closed policy, even if the minister will be making an annual statement. By devices within his department this statement will be kept a secret from the people of Canada.
As has been stated previously, we will vote against this bill because we do not believe that the immigration policies of this country should be decided as they will be, to a large extent, by the minister, the deputy minister, and officers of their department both inside and outside Canada. We believe prospective immigrants should be more aware of the reason why they were turned down. They should also be aware of the fact that they have the right to appeal. The appeal procedure should be easier than that found in the provisions of the bill as drafted.
This bill is deficient in view of the fact that it does not recognize the multicultural character of this country. For these various reasons, it is my intention to vote against this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House has finally come tonight to the conclusion of a long and interesting debate which has at last opposed people with very different views on the relations between the state and the citizen. I have deeply appreciated working in committee where cooperation as well as fair exchanges of views prevailed throughout the 70 hours of debate.
It is a fact, Mr. Speaker, that the work accomplished has brought a substantial improvement to the quality of this legislation introduced in the House of Commons by the government. Mr. Speaker, the minister pointed out during the debate at the report stage that the law had been improved. He insisted a lot on the number of amendments he had accepted. I think he mentioned that close to one hundred amendments were approved by the House and the committee and then sanctioned by the House but 1 would respectfully remind him that the number of amendments approved and passed are not necessarily an indication of a substantial improvement of this bill.
I was surprised last night to hear another minister on television, a minister representing another level of government, using exactly the same argument to try to explain that a famous legislation, a legislation in which a good many members of this House are quite interested, had been greatly improved because of some hundred amendments that had been accepted. I think what is important is the nature, the effect, the substance of these amendments, which give the real measure to determine whether a legislation has been improved or not.
Mr. Speaker, the issue of national security has been present throughout the whole debate. I will not elaborate too much on this, but I think that the difficult problem encountered and still present in any democratic system is to try to find a balance between the safeguard of our institutions and of democracy and the steps a government or the executive must take to protect the democratic system.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that Bill C-24 unfortunately contains in several of its provisions some factors which could give rise to rather serious abuses. I do not challenge nor question the good faith and the ideal which inspire this government. Being well acquainted with the cabinet members and the people who run the government, 1 do not think there is any problem for the time being. However, I think that to govern is essentially to anticipate and we must see that any bill passed
Immigration
by Parliament is drafted in such way that not only this government, but also the government of tomorrow or the day after tomorrow-since we are living under a democratic system and governments are replaced-but also future governments could not be in a position to take advantage of it, especially as far as national security is concerned, and open the door to abuses which could infringe the individual freedom of the Canadian people, the permanent residents and visitors.
Mr. Speaker, I would like more especially to quote a few examples. Amendments have been submitted, for example, to clause 39 which more specifically deal with visitors and security certificates. Under the proposed amendment, the security certificate should be issued at the discretion of a judge of the Federal Court, but since that amendment has been negatived, we are back to a situation where, essentially, the security certificates may be issued by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration and the Solicitor General, without any form of control whatsoever. The same goes with clause 40, where the Advisory Board provided for has advisory powers only, which means that whatever its verdict the excutive can always ignore it.
I would now like to say a few words about political refugees, which has been my main issue with Bill C-24 through all its stages. I would suggest once more to the minister, in a most friendly way, that on this matter 1 have the deep conviction that I have been defending not only a just cause but the right one. Because I cannot accept the point that widening the definition of "refugee" would have created problems as far as the refugee program administration is concerned. I feel that the special programs developed by the government in respect of certain countries such as Uganda or Chile could create as many problems strictly speaking, inasmuch as a great number of residents, citizens and nationals living in those countries could in theory seek political asylum in Canada. The key to this whole matter in my view lies in a distinction that has been ignored, the difference between admissibility and selection. Clearly, under the act a greater number of individuals could have been admissible as refugees, but on the other hand the possibility always remained with the government under the act itself, as is now the case, to select those who seemed to meet certain criteria. To conclude on the matter of political refugees, I am otherwise happy that the minister accepted to submit refugees to clause 6(2), so that special criteria would apply to those special immigrants. Mr. Speaker, important improvements have also been made in the committee, and I would like to speak about the matter of exit permits which, it seems to me, constituted an extremely dangerous initiative and opened the door to many potential abuses from which the Canadian democracy would inevitably have suffered in a few years.
Mr. Speaker, we could speak for hours about such a complex bill, but I would like to close by quoting the French poet Paul Valery since, as I said in the beginning, this bill essentially concerns the relationship between the state and the citizens. Valery said: If the state is strong, we are crushed, if it is weak, we perish. Therefore, in such a bill as this one, the objective

July 25, 1977
Immigration
that we should have aimed for, and I believe that we have missed it, should have been, on one hand, to establish a balance to enable the state to gain sufficient strength so that our democracy may endure and develop, and on the other hand, to protect the freedoms of the citizens of this country, and not only of the Canadian citizens, but also of all the people in the world who wish to come to Canada, either as immigrants or as visitors. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, it is the duty of members of this House to see to it that the legislative authority, the courts have some input in major decisions, and 1 believe that in Bill C-24, the legislative authority has been in a certain way short-circuited through a series of regulations. I am pleased that an amendment was made to clause 115, so that at least, before regulations are proclaimed in the Official Gazette, Parliament can be made aware of them.
